lessons.title: What Are Vitamins?
ingredient_words: vitamins A, C, D, E and K
lessons.summary:
This module is the starting point for the vitamin side of our range. It defines a vitamin as an organic compound the body
needs in small amounts and cannot make in sufficient quantities, so it must come from food, supplements or fortified
products. It splits vitamins into water-soluble ones, which are not stored and are needed regularly, and fat-soluble ones,
which are stored and can build up to toxic levels.

It then walks through what each vitamin does, explains why the alphabet has gaps (substances once called vitamins, such
as "vitamin H", were later reclassified or renamed), and introduces the forms a vitamin can take: provitamin, active,
synthetic and coenzyme. Bioavailability and conversion efficiency explain why form matters, especially for older people
or those with genetic variations such as MTHFR. Vitamins also work together, which matters when building a
multivitamin.

The last slide is the commercial point. Vitamins often need stabilising, coating or encapsulating, and the right choice
depends on the customer's delivery format, other ingredients, taste profile and budget or positioning. Knowing the
forms, and asking the right questions, is how we match an ingredient to a brief.
takeaways: Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small quantities that the body cannot produce in sufficient amounts; they act as coenzymes or antioxidants (slide 2).
Water-soluble vitamins are not stored in large amounts and are needed regularly; fat-soluble vitamins are stored in fatty tissue and can accumulate to toxic levels if taken in excess (slide 4).
Missing letters and out-of-order B numbers come from reclassification: "vitamin H" is now biotin (B7), "vitamin F" the essential fatty acids, "vitamin M" folic acid (slide 7).
Vitamins come as provitamins (beta-carotene to vitamin A), active forms (retinol), synthetic forms (folic acid) and coenzyme forms (methylcobalamin) (slide 8).
Bioavailability depends on the form, digestive health and nutrient interactions; conversion efficiency on genetics (MTHFR), age and health status (slide 10).
Vitamins work in synergy, for example vitamin D with calcium and vitamin C with non-heme iron, which matters when formulating multivitamins (slide 11).

- Expect to offer stabilised, coated or encapsulated forms: they change solubility, heat stability, bioavailability, oxidation stability and taste (slide 12).
- Customers still ask for old names such as "vitamin H"; the reclassification table lets you translate them (slide 7, speaker notes).
- Form is a selling point: the deck says people with certain conditions or who are ageing may benefit from active forms that bypass conversion (slide 10).
- My reading: the synergy pairs on slide 11 (D with calcium, B12 with folate, D with K2) are natural starting points for a premix conversation.

quiz.q: Why do fat-soluble vitamins carry a toxicity risk that water-soluble ones mostly do not?
quiz.a: They are stored in the body's fatty tissues and can accumulate to toxic levels if taken in excess; excess water-soluble vitamins are usually excreted in urine (slide 4).

quiz.q: A customer asks for "vitamin H". What do they mean?
quiz.a: Biotin, vitamin B7, recognised as part of the B-complex (slide 7).

quiz.q: What is the difference between folic acid and folate in the deck's terms?
quiz.a: Folic acid is the synthetic form of folate (vitamin B9): more stable in supplements, but it must be converted to the active form in the body (slide 8).

quiz.q: Name three factors that affect conversion efficiency.
quiz.a: Genetics (e.g. MTHFR variation and folic acid), age (e.g. beta-carotene to vitamin A, B12 conversion) and health status such as liver or kidney disease (slide 10).

quiz.q: What four things does the deck say may affect which vitamin form you recommend?
quiz.a: Delivery format, other ingredients, taste profile, and budget or brand positioning (slide 12).

sequence.script: This is the vitamins module from our Training and Development team: an introduction to what vitamins are and how to think about them. Each slide has a short explanation like this one, and there are two videos along the way. They open on YouTube in a new tab, so come back here when each one ends.

Vitamins are organic compounds that are essential in small amounts for various biological processes that sustain life. Unlike macronutrients like carbohydrates, proteins, or fats, which the body needs in larger quantities, vitamins are required in minute amounts to catalyze and regulate key biochemical reactions.

Since the human body either cannot synthesize these compounds at all or cannot produce them in sufficient amounts, vitamins must be obtained from external sources such as food, supplements, or fortified products.

Most vitamins act as coenzymes, meaning they assist enzymes in their role of catalyzing chemical reactions. Some vitamins also serve as antioxidants, helping to protect cells from damage caused by free radicals.

In the original deck this slide plays a video, and here it comes up as the next slide. It is "From Scurvy to Success: How Vitamins Revolutionized Modern Nutrition Science", from Dr. William Wallace's channel, and the link starts one minute twenty-three seconds in. It tells the story behind the definition we have just seen.
Watch from 1:23 for how deficiency diseases such as scurvy led to the idea of a vitamin. It is an outside channel's account, so take it as background, not as our wording.

sequence.script:
Vitamins are vital for maintaining overall health and preventing disease. Without them, the body cannot function properly. Each vitamin has specific roles, such as promoting energy metabolism, supporting immune function, aiding in cell and tissue repair, and contributing to neurological functions. Deficiencies in certain vitamins can lead to a range of health issues, from fatigue and weakened immunity to more serious conditions like scurvy, rickets, or neurological disorders.

For instance, Vitamin D is crucial for calcium absorption, which is essential for bone health, while Vitamin C plays a major role in collagen synthesis and immune support. The right balance of vitamins is essential for optimal well-being, energy, and longevity.

This slide and the next are reference tables: each vitamin, the benefits the deck lists, and a line on each. Here are the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, plus vitamin C, which is water-soluble. For example, vitamin A is listed for vision in low light, vitamin C for collagen formation, vitamin D for calcium absorption and bones, and vitamin K for blood clotting. Some lines here are still being checked as claim wording, so use the table to learn the roles, not as words for a customer.

This table covers the water-soluble B vitamins: B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9 and B12. Several are listed for energy metabolism, turning carbohydrates, fats and proteins into energy. B6 helps produce serotonin, dopamine and GABA. Folate, B9, is listed for DNA synthesis and repair, and B12 for red blood cell formation and normal nerve function. As with the last slide, some lines are still being checked as claim wording, so use it to learn the roles, not as words for a customer.

You might notice that some letters are missing in the sequence of vitamin names (e.g., there's no Vitamin F, H, or I).

This is because, as our understanding of these compounds evolved, some substances originally thought to be vitamins were later reclassified.

For example, what was once called "Vitamin F" is now known to be essential fatty acids (like Omega-3 and Omega-6).

Similarly, some vitamins were grouped together under a common name, such as the B-complex vitamins, which were originally thought to be individual vitamins.

It's important to be aware of some of this because even now, some people will ask us for Vitamin H, for example.

A vitamin can come in different forms, and the slide sets out four. Provitamins are converted by the body into the vitamin: beta-carotene becomes vitamin A. Active forms are ready to use, like retinol. Synthetic forms are made for stability or shelf life: folic acid, the synthetic form of folate, is more stable in supplements but must be converted in the body. Coenzyme forms, such as methylcobalamin for B12, need no further conversion; the deck describes it as more bioavailable than cyanocobalamin.

This slide holds the deck's second video, which comes up next: "Multivitamins: Should You Be Taking Them?", a nutritionist explaining on Myprotein's channel. It sits between the forms of vitamins we have just covered and the next slide, on how well the body absorbs and uses them.
Watch for how the nutritionist frames who might take a multivitamin and why. It comes from a brand's own channel, so treat it as a consumer view, not as our wording or claims.

sequence.script: Two ideas decide how well a vitamin works in the body. Bioavailability is how much is absorbed and used. It depends on the form, on digestive health, and on other nutrients: fat helps absorb vitamin D, while phytic acid in grains inhibits iron absorption. Conversion efficiency is how well the body turns a provitamin into its active form, and genetics, such as MTHFR with folic acid, age and health status all affect it. The slide's point: people with certain conditions, or who are ageing, may benefit from active forms.

Vitamins rarely work alone, and the slide calls this synergy: one nutrient supporting another. Vitamin D increases calcium absorption in the gut. Vitamin C enhances absorption of non-heme iron from plant foods. B12 and folate are both needed for DNA synthesis and red blood cell formation, and vitamin C regenerates vitamin E's antioxidant capacity. The second table pairs vitamins with other nutrients, such as vitamin A with zinc and B6 with magnesium. The deck's point for us: these pairings matter when formulating a multivitamin.

This is the commercial slide. Vitamins often need stabilising, and they can be attached to or encapsulated by other ingredients to change their solubility, heat stability, bioavailability, oxidation stability or taste. So start with the customer. What is the delivery format: a capsule, softgel, bulk tub, stick pack, liquid shot, carbonated drink, protein bar or brownie? What else is in it, what taste do they want, and what is the budget and positioning, basic or premium?

lessons.title: Amino Acids
lessons.summary:
This module builds amino acids up from first principles. An amino acid is an organic molecule with an amine group, a
carboxyl group and a side chain that is unique to each one; there are 20 standard amino acids. Linked by peptide bonds
they form peptides (2 to 50 amino acids) and, as longer folded chains, proteins, which the deck explains through the
four levels of protein structure.

It then sorts amino acids into essential, conditionally essential and non-essential groups, picks out the branched-chain
amino acids, and shows how they can also be grouped by charge and polarity. The second half is about use: synergies
with minerals (chelates such as magnesium bisglycinate), applications in animal feed, pet food, baking, flavour,
fortification, sports nutrition, nutricosmetics and dietary supplements, and the formulation issues that decide whether
a product works: heat, pH and oxidation stability, absorption, and the choice between free-form amino acids, peptides
and intact proteins.

It ends with plant-based blends and their limits. Combining pea and rice protein completes the amino acid profile, but a
blend of single amino acids has no peptide structure, so it cannot copy what hydrolysed collagen peptides do. That
distinction is what a colleague needs when customers ask about vegan alternatives.
takeaways: Amino acids are organic molecules with an amine group, a carboxyl group and a unique side chain; there are 20 standard amino acids (slide 4).
Amino acids are single units, peptides are chains of 2 to 50, and proteins are longer chains (generally over 50) folded into functional structures (slide 7).
Nine amino acids are essential, including the three BCAAs leucine, isoleucine and valine; the deck lists others as conditionally non-essential (e.g. arginine, glutamine) or non-essential (slide 13).

Amino acids degrade with heat, pH and oxidation (sulfur amino acids such as methionine and cysteine are most vulnerable); microencapsulation, freeze-drying and liposomal encapsulation protect them (slide 29).
Free-form amino acids absorb fastest, peptides balance speed and sustained release, and intact proteins absorb slowest; amino acids can compete for the same absorption pathways (slide 29).
Plant blends such as pea plus rice protein complete the amino acid profile, but single amino acid blends lack the peptide functionality of hydrolysed collagen (slide 30) (slide 31).
lessons.in_practice:
- When a customer asks for a vegan collagen, explain the deck's point: a plant amino acid blend can match collagen's profile but not its peptides, so it cannot mimic their structure or bioactivity (slide 31).
- Match the form to the product: free-form for rapid absorption in sports and recovery products, peptides such as collagen peptides for balance, intact proteins for sustained release (slide 29).
- Raise stability early: high heat can degrade glutamine and lysine, glutamine degrades in acidic environments, and many amino acids are hygroscopic, which affects shelf life (slide 29).
- Chelation (e.g. magnesium bisglycinate) is the deck's example of amino acids improving mineral absorption and stability (slide 18).
- My reading: the feed, pet food and baking slides (20 to 25) are context on where the bulk of amino acid demand sits rather than our own markets.

quiz.a: An amine group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH) and a side chain (R-group) unique to each amino acid (slide 4).

quiz.q: How does the deck distinguish peptides from proteins?
quiz.a: Peptides are chains of 2 to 50 amino acids; proteins are long chains, generally over 50, folded into functional structures (slide 7).

quiz.a: It is a blend of individual amino acids with no peptide functionality, so it cannot mimic collagen's peptides or their structural support (slide 31).

sequence.script: Welcome to this module on amino acids. Amino acids sit behind many of the ingredients we talk about every day, so it's worth knowing the basics well. The next slide sets out the agenda and what you'll learn; after that, we start with what an amino acid actually is.

Welcome to the training session on amino acids.

Over the next 40 minutes or so, we’re going to explore amino acids from the ground up—what they are, why they’re essential for human health, and how they’re used in various parts of the food and fitness industries.

As always, this is quite foundational, but I've also tried to tie in some data and trends stuff which is hopefully more advanced. So, whether you’re already familiar with amino acids or starting from scratch, this session should provide a newer and deeper understanding to some degree.

We’ll start with the basics: defining amino acids and their role in the body. Then, we’ll move into the differences between amino acids, peptides, and proteins—explaining how these compounds interact to support biological functions.

After that, we’ll delve into the key categories of amino acids, including essential amino acids (EAAs), branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), and others like conditional amino acids. Understanding these distinctions is critical for identifying their applications.

Finally, we’ll discuss amino acid trends, market insights, and how the science of amino acids is advancing in terms of stability, bioavailability, and formulation innovations.

By the end of this session, you’ll not only understand amino acids but also the key industry areas where they’re making an impact and how we might see demand and supply evolve in the coming years.

Part one: an introduction to amino acids. In this section we'll cover what an amino acid is, the jobs amino acids do in the body, and how single amino acids link up into peptides and then proteins. There are two short videos along the way that show this in action.

Amino acids are often called the building blocks of life because they are fundamental to almost every biological process in the body.

At their core, amino acids are organic molecules with three key components: an amine group (-NH₂), a carboxyl group (-COOH), and a side chain or R-group that is unique to each amino acid.

It’s this side chain that determines the specific properties and functions of each amino acid.

Amino acids serve as the foundation for two critical biological structures: peptides and proteins.

When two or more amino acids link together, they form peptides. When these peptides grow into longer chains—50 or more amino acids—they become proteins, which fold into complex structures to carry out a wide range of functions in the body.

These functions include building and repairing tissues, acting as enzymes and hormones, and even supporting the immune system. Without amino acids, processes like muscle repair, energy production, and neurotransmitter synthesis simply wouldn’t happen.

Importantly, amino acids are classified based on how we obtain them. Some are essential, meaning we must get them from food or supplements because the body can’t produce them. Others are non-essential, which the body can produce on its own. There’s also a category called conditional amino acids, which are usually non-essential but become essential in times of illness or stress.

Understanding these basic properties is the foundation for exploring how amino acids are used in nutrition, health, and various industries.

This chart shows the 20 common amino acids, each with its name, its three-letter code and its one-letter code. They all share the same backbone: an amine group and a carboxyl group. What changes is the side chain, drawn in colour. The colours sort them by side chain: aliphatic, aromatic, amidic, hydroxylic, negatively or positively charged, and sulphur-containing. You don't need to learn the structures; just notice that the side chain gives each amino acid its character.

sequence.script:
To fully understand amino acids, it’s important to see how they relate to peptides and proteins.

Amino acids are the smallest structural units in this hierarchy, but when they link together, they form peptides—chains of 2 to 50 amino acids held together by peptide bonds.

These peptide bonds are formed through a process called dehydration synthesis, where a molecule of water is removed as the amino acids join together.

When these peptide chains grow larger, typically containing more than 50 amino acids, they fold into complex three-dimensional structures to form proteins.

Proteins are the workhorses of the body, responsible for countless vital functions, including acting as enzymes, transporting molecules, and providing structural support in tissues like muscles and skin.

The differences between amino acids, peptides, and proteins largely come down to size and complexity: Amino acids are individual units. Peptides are shorter chains of amino acids. Proteins are long, folded chains with specific shapes that determine their functions.

It's also important to note that the structure of any protein - and therefore its function - is defined by its amino acid and peptide structure, and that variations of these can give us truly unique protein forms and applications, such as: Linear proteins like collagen provide structure to skin and connective tissue. Globular proteins like hemoglobin transport oxygen in the blood. Enzymatic proteins catalyze reactions critical for life.

This hierarchy—amino acids to peptides to proteins—is fundamental to how the body works. Proteins are responsible for tasks as diverse as building muscle, repairing tissues, and transporting molecules. Understanding this relationship provides a foundation for exploring their applications in health and nutrition.

This slide is another video, from Dr Matt and Dr Mike, on proteins and amino acids. It goes over the same ground as the last slide, amino acids, peptides and proteins, with the biochemistry drawn out step by step. Watch it before we move on to protein structure.

Next, a short biochemistry lesson from Dr Matt and Dr Mike on proteins and amino acids. Watch for the difference between amino acids, peptides and proteins, and how a chain folds into a working shape.

Here is the chart of the 20 common amino acids again, as we move on to how proteins are built. Keep the side chains in mind: each amino acid's side chain is different, and the next slides show how the order of amino acids in a chain leads to the folded shapes that give proteins their jobs.

Proteins are organized into four levels of structure, each adding complexity and defining function. The primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids, which sets the foundation for the protein’s identity. This sequence folds into secondary structures, like alpha helices or beta sheets, stabilized by hydrogen bonds.

Next, the tertiary structure forms when the chain folds into a specific 3D shape. This is where proteins take on their functional forms, like enzymes or hormones. Finally, some proteins form quaternary structures, where multiple folded chains combine into complexes, such as hemoglobin for oxygen transport or collagen in connective tissues.

These structural levels define the protein’s role—whether it’s a globular enzyme driving a chemical reaction or a fibrous protein providing strength to muscles or skin. This hierarchical design makes proteins incredibly versatile, supporting diverse industries like nutrition, beauty, and medicine.

This slide shows how the amino acid chain shapes the finished protein. Top left are three shapes: fibrous, like collagen; globular, like prolegumin; and random-coil, like casein. Below, collagen is built up from amino acid chains rich in glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, twisted into triple helices, then fibrils and fibres. On the right is an enzyme: forces between its amino acids hold the shape of its active site, and high temperatures can break those forces so the substrate no longer fits.

Part two: the categories and biochemistry of amino acids. Here we sort amino acids into groups, essential, conditionally non-essential and non-essential, take a closer look at the branched-chain amino acids, and then see how their chemistry sets them apart. Two short videos in this section help with both topics.

Amino acids are categorized based on how the body obtains and uses them, as well as their chemical properties.

The first grouping is essential amino acids (EAAs), which must be obtained through diet or supplementation because the body cannot produce them.

These include leucine, isoleucine, and valine—known as branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)—which are key for muscle repair and energy.

Non-essential amino acids, like alanine and aspartic acid, are produced by the body and support basic metabolic functions.

There are also conditional amino acids. Conditionally essential amino acids are a unique group. Under normal circumstances, the body can produce them in sufficient amounts, so they’re classified as non-essential. However, in certain situations—like illness, stress, or intense physical activity—the body’s demand for these amino acids increases beyond what it can synthesize. This is when they become ‘conditionally essential’ and must be obtained from diet or supplements.

For example, glutamine is important for gut health and immune function. During periods of illness or injury, the body’s need for glutamine increases, making dietary intake critical. Similarly, arginine plays a role in wound healing and nitric oxide production, which supports blood flow. During stress or trauma, the body cannot produce enough to meet its needs.

This concept is especially important in medical nutrition and sports recovery. Products targeting gut health, immune support, or post-exercise recovery often include these amino acids to meet the body’s heightened demands.

I've put a short list of the 9 essential aminos, and some of their primary functions at the side here - as you can see, they are responsible for all sorts of important biological functions, from immunity, to muscle repair, to the health of our brain and nervous system, and more.

I've also broken out BCAAs - that's branched chain amino acids - to show you their structure here. As you can see, the functional R group of each amino acid (that's the green section) has at least one branch in it off a carbon, and that structure gives us the 'branched chain' name.

sequence.script:
I won't focus too much on this, because a video earlier started to explain it quite well, but we can additionally classify amino acids by their chemical properties, such as polarity, charge, or structural groupings.

For example, some amino acids are hydrophobic, like leucine, while others are hydrophilic, like serine, affecting how they interact in proteins and the body.

Building on this, we can also classify amino acids by their charge and acidity. For instance, acidic amino acids, like aspartic acid and glutamic acid, have negatively charged side chains, while basic amino acids, like lysine and arginine, carry a positive charge. These properties influence how amino acids behave in different environments, such as binding to other molecules or stabilizing protein structures.

Another grouping considers the structure of the side chains. Aromatic amino acids, like phenylalanine and tyrosine, contain ring structures, making them critical in protein signaling and interactions.

These chemical distinctions are key when designing formulations or targeting specific physiological functions. Understanding these categories allows us to design products tailored to specific health and performance needs.

sequence.script: Part three: science, function and formulation. This section covers how amino acids work with other nutrients such as minerals, where they're used today across food, feed, beauty and supplements, how stable and bioavailable they are in a finished product, and what's new, from plant-based blends to targeted delivery.

Amino acids don’t just work alone—they interact with other nutrients and compounds to enhance their effectiveness. One important synergy is between amino acids and minerals. For example, chelated minerals are formed when amino acids bind to minerals like magnesium or zinc, improving both stability and absorption. These chelates are widely used in supplements to enhance bioavailability.

Amino acids also play critical roles in enzymatic and metabolic processes. Arginine, for instance, supports nitric oxide production, which improves blood flow and is a key component in sports and cardiovascular health products. Similarly, glutamine aids gut health by serving as a fuel source for intestinal cells.

Another functional aspect is how amino acids influence protein synthesis. Leucine, a branched-chain amino acid, is known for its ability to trigger muscle protein synthesis, making it essential in sports recovery products. These synergies and functions make amino acids indispensable in developing targeted health and performance solutions.

Amino acids are at the heart of many functional products across industries. In sports nutrition, essential amino acids (EAAs) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) are staples for muscle repair, endurance, and recovery. Leucine, for instance, plays a key role in stimulating muscle protein synthesis, making it a common ingredient in post-workout supplements.

For gut health, glutamine is widely used to support intestinal integrity and repair, especially in products targeting digestive wellness or recovery from illness.

In the beauty sector, amino acids like glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline are key components in collagen supplements, promoting skin elasticity and hydration. They’re also used in nutricosmetics, where ‘beauty-from-within’ solutions are increasingly popular.

In cognitive health, amino acids like tryptophan and tyrosine are used to support neurotransmitter production, influencing mood and focus. These applications highlight the versatility of amino acids in addressing a wide range of health needs.

Amino acids aren't only for people. In animal feed, lysine, methionine, threonine and tryptophan are added to balance protein in feed formulations, including low-protein diets, to improve feed conversion: more meat, milk or eggs per unit of feed. The slide lists the benefits as cost efficiency, lower nitrogen excretion and support for animal health. Trends to watch: plant-based or fermentation-derived amino acids in feed, and premixes tailored to species and growth stage.

It splits the market by application, from ruminants, poultry and swine to pets, equine and aqua; by product, such as tryptophan, lysine, methionine and threonine; and by region. The key findings it names are a push to improve livestock quality and progress in biotechnology.
Taurine is essential for cats because they cannot synthesize it; deficiency can lead to heart disease and vision loss.

In baking, amino acids work as processing aids. L-cysteine acts as a dough conditioner, improving elasticity and cutting mixing time; methionine supports yeast fermentation for better volume and texture; and proline helps stabilise the gluten structure. The slide lists the results: more consistent dough, better texture and shelf life, and shorter baking times. Amino acids also help gluten-free products mimic the elasticity of gluten, and plant-based amino acids are part of clean-label baking.
Glutamic acid is the key driver of the umami flavor, often referred to as the 'fifth taste.'

Fortification is about filling gaps. Lysine is added to cereals and grains, and methionine to plant-based proteins, to complete their amino acid profiles. The slide also lists tryptophan in fortified foods aimed at mood and sleep, and glutamine in meal replacements. Uses run from staples like rice, wheat and corn in regions with protein malnutrition, to protein bars, cereals and shakes. The trends: fortified plant-based foods for flexitarians and vegans, and biofortified crops.
Leucine is the most potent BCAA for muscle protein synthesis, making it a key ingredient in recovery products.

In beauty, amino acids turn up both in supplements and on the skin. Glycine, proline and hydroxyproline are components of collagen, which is why they matter for collagen supplements sold as beauty from within. Cysteine and methionine supply sulphur for keratin, so they appear in hair and nail products, and the slide lists arginine for the skin's microcirculation. You'll also find amino acids in creams and serums. Trends include plant-based collagen analogues, vegan beauty products and nutricosmetics that target hair, skin and nails together.

In supplements, amino acids are grouped by need. For sleep, the slide lists tryptophan, a precursor to serotonin and melatonin, and glycine. For cognitive health, tyrosine and tryptophan, linked to dopamine and serotonin. For gut health, glutamine and proline. For immune support, arginine and cysteine, a precursor to glutathione. The trends it names are natural, non-habit-forming solutions, personalised formulas for gut, sleep and immune health, and products that combine several benefits.

Stability and bioavailability are critical factors when it comes to amino acids. Stability refers to how well an amino acid retains its structure and function during storage, processing, and digestion. Some amino acids, like glutamine, are prone to degradation in high heat or acidic environments, which can reduce their effectiveness in formulations.

Bioavailability, on the other hand, measures how efficiently the body absorbs and uses an amino acid. Free-form amino acids, which don’t need to be digested into smaller units, are highly bioavailable and are often used in supplements for rapid absorption. However, amino acids in complex proteins may require longer digestion, impacting the speed at which they become available to the body.

To address these challenges, technologies like microencapsulation protect amino acids from environmental factors, enhancing their stability. Other approaches, like pairing amino acids with minerals in chelated forms, not only improve stability but also enhance the absorption of both components. These innovations allow amino acids to be used effectively across diverse applications, from functional foods to advanced supplements.

Plant-based amino acid blends are increasingly popular as sustainable and ethical alternatives to animal-based proteins. The challenge with plant proteins, like pea or rice protein, is that they often lack one or more essential amino acids, making them incomplete proteins. To overcome this, blends of complementary plant proteins are used to mimic the amino acid profiles of animal proteins, ensuring a balanced intake.

For example, pea protein is high in lysine but low in methionine, while rice protein is the opposite. Combining these two creates a complete amino acid profile, comparable to whey or egg protein. These blends are commonly found in vegan protein powders, snacks, and meal replacements.

Beyond basic nutrition, plant-based amino acids are used to develop analogues of functional proteins like collagen. By isolating and combining specific amino acids, companies can replicate the benefits of animal-derived products while catering to plant-based consumers. This innovation is driving growth in plant-based markets, particularly in sports nutrition and beauty.

While plant-based amino acid blends can replicate the amino acid profile of animal-derived proteins like hydrolyzed collagen, they face significant limitations.

Hydrolyzed collagen is composed of peptides—short chains of amino acids—that have unique structural and functional properties. These peptides are responsible for collagen’s benefits, such as promoting skin elasticity, hydration, and joint health.

A blend of single amino acids, even with the same profile as collagen, does not have the same peptide structure. This lack of structure means it cannot mimic the bioactivity of true collagen peptides, such as their ability to stimulate collagen production in the skin or provide structural support in connective tissues.

Additionally, plant-based sources often require significant processing to isolate and combine amino acids, which can impact cost, sustainability, and scalability. While these blends are a step forward in offering alternatives to animal-derived collagen, they are not yet able to fully replace the functional benefits of true collagen peptides.

The science of amino acids continues to evolve, leading to new innovations in stability, delivery, and functionality. One key area of development is in targeted delivery systems, such as liposomal or enteric-coated amino acids. These technologies protect amino acids as they pass through the digestive system, ensuring they reach the intended site of absorption, like the intestines, for maximum effectiveness.

Another innovation is in fermentation-derived amino acids, which provide a sustainable and scalable alternative to traditional extraction methods. This process is particularly important for amino acids like tryptophan and lysine, which are challenging to source naturally at scale.

We’re also seeing advancements in amino acid blends for functional applications, such as analogues for specialty proteins. For instance, companies are working on plant-based alternatives to whey protein and collagen that incorporate optimized amino acid profiles for improved functionality and taste.

Lastly, research is focusing on the synergistic effects of amino acids with other nutrients. For example, amino acids are being combined with probiotics or minerals to enhance both stability and bioavailability in gut health and sports nutrition products. These innovations are opening up exciting possibilities for amino acids in personalized health and wellness.

To wrap up, amino acids are essential building blocks of life, with applications that extend far beyond basic nutrition. We’ve explored their foundational role in peptides and proteins, their classifications, and their structural importance. We’ve also discussed how their stability and bioavailability can be enhanced through innovative technologies like microencapsulation and targeted delivery systems.

In industry, amino acids play critical roles across diverse sectors—from sports nutrition and beauty to gut health and even cognitive support. Emerging trends, such as sustainable fermentation and plant-based analogues, highlight the versatility and growing importance of amino acids in meeting consumer demands for health, functionality, and sustainability.

As amino acid science continues to evolve, the potential for innovation in formulation, personalization, and applications will only expand. By understanding their properties and functions, we can create products that address specific health needs while staying at the forefront of industry trends.

lessons.title: Prebiotics & Fibre: The Comprehensive Commercial Curriculum
lessons.summary:
This module is the commercial team's grounding in dietary fibre and prebiotics. It starts with demand: most adults fall well
short of recommended fibre intake, and a cultural wave (fibermaxxing, GLP-1) and a surge of new products sit on top of that
need. It then separates two words customers often blur. Fibre is a compositional category with legal definitions and a number
on the label. Prebiotic is a function that must be shown, and in the EU and UK the word itself is treated as an implied health
claim. The deck keeps soluble versus insoluble as a first sort, then adds three dials (viscosity, fermentability and chain
length) that predict what a fibre does, including how much gas it causes. Each ingredient is graded Gold, Silver or Bronze on
its human evidence, kept apart from whether it is a recognised prebiotic and whether a claim can go on pack. Formulation dials
(dose, taste, ease of use, stability) decide whether an ingredient fits a format at all. The module ends with the authorised
claims list, a quick-pick by customer brief, a five-link decision chain and our H2 2026 priorities: the precision-prebiotic end,
the GLP-1 companion, credibility, and HMO supply.
takeaways: The fibre gap is the demand driver: about 5% of men and 9% of women reach recommended daily fibre, a shortfall of about 14 g a day (16 g actual against 25–38 g), on US data (slide 2).
"Fibre" is a regulated number you can almost always put on a panel; "prebiotic" is a claim you must earn, and in the EU, UK and Canada it is an implied health claim (slide 26).

Solubility alone predicts little. Viscosity predicts cholesterol and glucose effects, fermentability predicts SCFAs and gas, and chain length predicts the speed and site of fermentation, so tolerability (slide 11).

Keep three questions apart: is it a recognised prebiotic, how strong is the human evidence for this benefit (Gold, Silver, Bronze), and can we say it on pack here (slide 17). Inulin, FOS and GOS are the deck's "only three you can call prebiotic with full confidence", and GOS works at much lower doses (slide 19).

Gentle is a selling point: inulin and FOS are gas-prone with a tolerance ceiling of about 5–10 g a day in one serving, while PHGG, acacia and resistant maltodextrin are fermented slowly and suit the sensitive-gut segment (slide 12).
Every decision runs through one chain: claim, evidence, dose, format, jurisdiction. If any link breaks, the claim breaks (slide 36).
lessons.in_practice:
- Keep the quick-pick open in a customer meeting: GOS, XOS or RS2 for a low-dose capsule, gummy or small drink; soluble corn
  fibre, resistant wheat dextrin, resistant maltodextrin or GOS for a clear drink; PHGG, acacia or low-dose XOS for sensitive gut
  and low-FODMAP; oat β-glucan or psyllium for a cardiometabolic claim (slide 35).
- When the brief is cholesterol or glucose, go to the viscous fibres with authorised claims; the deck says not to reach for
  inulin, FOS, acacia or wheat dextrin there, as they lack the mechanism (slide 22).
- When a claim must survive a regulator or a retailer's legal team, anchor it in the authorised claims list and quote the dose
  (slides 27, 32).
- Pick the ingredient that is good enough on every dial, not the best on one: the deck's worked example chose PHGG with GOS
  because both were low-dose, clinically validated, near-tasteless and easy to use (slide 24).
- For GLP-1 users, fibre has two roles: managing GI side effects and the "fibre-first" natural GLP-1 secretion story
  (slide 29). The deck's gentle picks for a GLP-1 companion are PHGG, acacia gum and resistant dextrins (slide 35).
- Use market sizes to size an opportunity, not to forecast; the deck says estimates vary two to three times (slide 28).
lessons.detail:
**Definitions.** Codex (2009) counts fibre from DP 10 and leaves DP 3–9 to national authorities; the US FDA (2016) and EU/UK
(Regulation 1169/2011) count from DP 3, and the FDA requires isolated or synthetic fibres to show a physiological benefit. The
deck's key point: whether microbes selectively use a fibre is irrelevant to fibre status (slide 4). For prebiotics the
scientific reference is ISAPP 2017 ("a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health
benefit"); the deck adopts the GPA 2024 definition as our operating one, which drops the selectivity test and adds performance
benefits, so ingredients such as polyphenols can be credited with a "prebiotic effect" (slide 5). The biotic family is set out
by contrast: probiotic (Hill 2014), prebiotic (ISAPP 2017), synbiotic (ISAPP 2020) and postbiotic (ISAPP 2021) (slide 6). In the
Venn diagram, lactulose, HMOs, polyphenols and omega-3 sit outside fibre: lactulose is too small (DP 2), HMO fibre status is
contested, and polyphenols and omega-3 are not carbohydrates (slide 7).

**Mechanism.** Fibre escapes digestion in the small intestine and is fermented in the colon into short-chain fatty acids
(slide 9). Butyrate fuels colon cells and supports the gut barrier; propionate goes to the liver; acetate is the most abundant
and reaches the circulation. The deck links SCFAs to satiety hormones (GLP-1, PYY via FFAR2/FFAR3), immunity and the gut-brain
axis, and notes that some of these effects are better established than others (slide 10).

**Taxonomy and hard cases.** Two tables classify the common fibres by solubility, viscosity, fermentability and prebiotic status
(slides 14-15). The hard cases: methylcellulose is soluble and viscous but not fermented, so not a prebiotic; glucomannan is the
most viscous common fibre; acacia is soluble but non-viscous and very well tolerated; lignin is not a carbohydrate. IMO is "the
trap": much of it is digested and an FDA petition was denied. Resistant starch has five subtypes (RS1-RS5), and the deck says to
specify the type when claiming (slides 15-16).

**Evidence tiers, as the deck gives them.** Gold: psyllium (Jovanovski 2018, 28 RCTs, about 10 g a day lowered LDL by 0.33
mmol/L; dose 7–10 g a day with at least 250 mL water) and oat or barley β-glucan (Ho 2016, 58 RCTs, 3.5 g a day: LDL −4.2%;
competitor brands OatWell, PromOat) (slide 18); inulin (5–20 g a day; Orafti, Fibruline), FOS (5–21 g a day; Parnell and Reimer
2009, 21 g a day, −1.03 kg over 12 weeks; Orafti P95, Frutalose) and GOS (1.4–7 g a day; Bimuno, Vivinal/Biotis, Oligomate)
(slide 19). Silver: resistant starch (200+ human trials but heterogeneous; Hi-Maize/VersaFibe, Fibersym RW4, Solnul) and PHGG
(RCT n=108 on bloating; 5–7 g a day; Sunfiber) (slide 20). Bronze: XOS (Finegold 2014, 1.4–2.8 g a day; PreticX, Longlive),
AXOS (about 10 g a day; NAXUS, Arrabina), larch arabinogalactan (Riede 2013, 4.5 g a day; ResistAid) and native guar, which
the deck says PHGG has largely superseded (slide 21). Bronze means the breadth of human evidence is thin, not that it does not
work. The master tables (slides 30-31) add resistant dextrin, resistant maltodextrin, polydextrose, acacia, pectin, glucomannan,
lactulose, wheat dextrin, HMOs and branded botanicals (Solnul, AlphaGOS, Actazin/Livaux, Eldercraft, 360GUT, Baobest), with the
note to annotate each one's real benefit.

**Formulation.** Effective dose, taste, ease of use and stability decide fit: a 10 g fibre will not fit a capsule, gummy or
small drink (slide 23). Gas is "the silent compliance-killer", and a product nobody can tolerate is not bought again (slide 25).

**Claims.** The authorised list (slide 32): oat or barley β-glucan for cholesterol and CHD risk (FDA 1997, EFSA 2010; at least
3 g a day) and post-prandial glycaemia (EFSA; 4 g per 30 g carbohydrate); psyllium for CHD risk (FDA 1998; at least 7 g a day
soluble fibre); pectin for normal blood cholesterol (EFSA 2010; at least 6 g a day) and post-prandial glycaemia (at least 10 g
per meal); glucomannan for weight loss in a calorie-restricted diet (EFSA 2010; 3 g a day as 1 g three times); chicory inulin
for normal defecation and stool frequency (EU Reg. 2015/2314; at least 12 g a day); high-amylose maize RS2 "may reduce risk of
type 2 diabetes" (FDA 2016, qualified). Only the EFSA and EU entries apply to European packs.

**Market.** Prebiotics $6–11B and dietary fibre $9–14B (Grand View; FMI). Estimates vary two to three times depending on
whether ingredient or finished product and animal feed are counted; inulin is the largest single prebiotic (about 30–46% share),
gut health the largest segment, and Europe (about 40%) and APAC vie for the lead (slide 28). On GLP-1: about 30M+ US adults have
taken a GLP-1 (about 18%; 12% currently), digestive supplements among GLP-1 users +52% and weight-management formulas −3%
year on year; the slide names no source (slide 29).

**Reference tables.** Slides 33-34 reproduce the GPA table of established, novel and emerging prebiotics with doses and study
outcomes from Deehan et al., Advances in Nutrition 2024;15:100329, Table 1 (open access, CC BY 4.0; attribution required).

**Our H2 2026 priorities.** Lead at the precision-prebiotic end (low-dose, validated, palatable, blendable: PHGG, GOS, scFOS,
XOS and novel polyphenols, while commodity inulin and FOS keep the volume); build the GLP-1 companion; make credibility the moat
(honest dosing, evidence-matched claims, branded clinical ingredients); secure precision-fermentation supply of HMOs ahead of
adult-nutrition expansion (slide 37).

The conference library has related talks on fibre, the microbiome and GLP-1; further reading is linked automatically from the
shared tags.

quiz.q: Why can we almost always say "X g of fibre" on a pack but not "prebiotic" in the EU?
quiz.a: Fibre is a regulated, quantifiable label term defined by FDA, Codex and the EU; "prebiotic" is not a regulated nutrient claim, and in the EU, UK and Canada it is an implied health claim (slide 26)

quiz.q: A customer wants a cholesterol claim. Should we offer inulin or oat β-glucan, and why?
quiz.a: Oat β-glucan, which has FDA and EFSA claims at 3 g a day or more; inulin is non-viscous and lacks the mechanism (slide 22)

quiz.q: Which three questions does the grading method keep separate?
quiz.a: Prebiotic status, benefit-evidence depth (Gold, Silver, Bronze) and claimability on pack (slide 17)

quiz.q: What is the practical tolerance ceiling for rapidly fermented short-chain prebiotics, and name two ways round it?
quiz.a: About 5–10 g a day in a single serving; blend short and long chain, use slow or well-tolerated fibres, use low-dose-effective ingredients or escalate the dose gradually (slide 25)

quiz.q: What are the five links of the decision chain?
quiz.a: Claim, evidence, dose, format and jurisdiction; if any link breaks, the claim breaks (slide 36)

sequence.script: This is our commercial curriculum on prebiotics and fibre, written for the commercial team in the second half of 2026. Its aim is category fluency. It runs through definitions, mechanism, evidence, formulation, claims, the market and the ingredients themselves, and it ends with a decision framework and our priorities for the half.

Everything starts with the fibre gap. In the US data on this slide, about 5% of men and 9% of women reach the recommended daily fibre, a shortfall of about 14 grams: 16 grams eaten against 25 to 38 recommended. The deck cites a WHO-commissioned Lancet review from 2019, Reynolds and colleagues, which pooled 185 observational studies and 58 trials and reported lower death and disease rates, by 5 to 27%, with every extra 8 grams a day.

The deck sums up demand as a perfect storm of three forces. First, a real need: the fibre gap, which is structural and backed by the Lancet review. Second, a cultural wave: fibremaxxing, GLP-1 drugs, and the idea that "fibre is the new protein". Third, a product explosion: sodas, snacks and blends, and billion-dollar exits. Together, the deck says, they make durable demand and a growth opportunity.

What counts as fibre? The test is that it is not digested in the small intestine and, for isolated or added fibres, shows a physiological benefit. The definitions differ on chain length. Codex sets a degree of polymerisation of 10 or more and leaves 3 to 9 to national authorities. The US FDA and the EU and UK both use 3 or more. Note the key point: whether microbes selectively use it does not matter for fibre status.

What is a prebiotic? The scientific reference is ISAPP's 2017 definition: a substrate selectively used by host microorganisms, giving a health benefit. The one we operate on is the Global Prebiotic Association's 2024 definition: a compound used by the microbiota, producing a health or performance benefit. It drops the strict selectivity test and adds performance. That lets us credit ingredients such as polyphenols with a prebiotic effect without forcing the label "prebiotic" on them.

The biotic family is easiest to learn by contrast. Probiotics are live microorganisms that, in adequate amounts, confer a benefit: "the bugs". Prebiotics are the substrate those microbes use: "food for the host's bugs". Synbiotics combine the two. Postbiotics are inanimate microbes and their parts: "the spent bugs". Note that purified metabolites alone do not qualify as postbiotics.

This Venn diagram is the centrepiece. Some things are fibre only: cellulose, wheat bran, lignin, psyllium. Some are both: inulin, FOS and GOS. And some are prebiotic but not classic fibre. Lactulose is too small to count as fibre. HMOs feed infant bifidobacteria, but their fibre status is contested. Polyphenols and omega-3 are not carbohydrates at all, which is why the prebiotic circle reaches outside the fibre umbrella.

Start with the model customers already know: soluble and insoluble. Soluble fibre dissolves in water, often forming a gel, and slows digestion; the slide's list also mentions blood sugar and cholesterol, which later slides tie to specific viscous fibres at set doses. Insoluble fibre does not dissolve; it adds bulk and speeds transit. The standard advice is to eat a mix. It is a real, lab-measured distinction and a useful first cut, and the course builds on it.

Follow fibre through the gut. In the mouth and small intestine our enzymes break down starch and sugars, which are absorbed there. Fibre's bonds resist those enzymes, so it passes through intact. In the colon, trillions of microbes carry the enzymes we lack and ferment what arrives, producing short-chain fatty acids. So the colon, not the stomach, is the reaction vessel.

The deck says one chain explains most of the benefits we sell. Microbes make three short-chain fatty acids. Butyrate is the preferred fuel for the cells lining the colon. Propionate goes to the liver. Acetate, the most abundant, enters the circulation. From there the deck traces links to satiety hormones, since SCFAs can stimulate GLP-1 and PYY, to immunity and to the gut-brain axis. As the slide itself says, some of these effects are better established than others.

Four dials predict what a fibre will do. Solubility is the familiar starting point but a weak predictor on its own. Viscosity, whether it forms a gel, predicts cholesterol and glucose effects, as with beta-glucan, psyllium and guar. Fermentability predicts SCFAs and gas, as with inulin and FOS. Chain length predicts how fast and where it ferments, and so how well it is tolerated. When a customer asks what a fibre will do, reason through these dials.

Tolerability is a design lever. Fast, short-chain fibres such as inulin and FOS are powerful but gas-prone, with a ceiling of about 5 to 10 grams a day in a single serving. Slow or partly fermented fibres, such as PHGG, acacia and resistant maltodextrin or soluble corn fibre, are gentler, which opens the sensitive-gut, IBS-adjacent and low-FODMAP segment. Match ferment speed to the customer. Gentle is a feature: sell it.

There are four ways to classify fibre, and each predicts something different. Soluble versus insoluble is traditional and measurable, a useful first guide. Viscous versus non-viscous is linked to satiety and to cholesterol and glucose benefits. Fermentable or not is linked to microbiome benefits and to gas. Origin, whether intact, isolated or synthetic, matters for clean-label and sourcing questions, such as vegan or organic. Use viscosity and fermentability as the working lenses.

This is the first half of the fibre taxonomy: the structural, viscous and gel-forming fibres. For each one the table gives what it is, then whether it is soluble, viscous, fermentable and prebiotic. Cellulose, lignin and wheat bran are insoluble and not prebiotic. Beta-glucan and pectin are soluble gels. Psyllium forms a gel but resists fermentation. Glucomannan has the highest viscosity. Keep this table to hand rather than memorising it.

The second half covers the fermentable and oligosaccharide fibres, the prebiotic end. Inulin, FOS and GOS are soluble, rapidly fermented and established prebiotics. Resistant starch, acacia and PHGG are also listed as established. Resistant maltodextrin and polydextrose are slower to ferment and graded novel. The same columns apply: soluble, viscous, fermentable, prebiotic, so you can compare any two fibres at a glance.

These are the cases that trip people up. Methylcellulose is soluble and viscous but not fermented, so it is not a prebiotic. Glucomannan is the most viscous common fibre, with minimal prebiotic effect. Acacia is soluble but not viscous, slowly fermented and very well tolerated. Lignin is not a carbohydrate at all. And resistant starch has five subtypes, RS1 to RS5, so always specify the type when claiming.

The deck grades evidence Gold, Silver or Bronze. Gold means a large body of good human trials or meta-analyses and, or, authorised health claims. Silver means moderate, growing human evidence. Bronze means limited or emerging evidence. Keep three questions apart: is it a recognised prebiotic, how strong is the human evidence for this particular benefit, and can we use the word on pack here? Clinical evidence is not the same as commercial maturity.

The first Gold tier is psyllium and oat or barley beta-glucan, the regulator-backed viscous fibres. Psyllium: a review of 28 trials found about 10 grams a day lowered LDL by 0.33 millimoles per litre; the dose is 7 to 10 grams with at least 250 millilitres of water. Beta-glucan carries FDA and EFSA cholesterol claims at 3 grams a day or more. Neither is a prebiotic: the effect is physical, and the claim only holds at the dose.

The second Gold tier is the three proven prebiotics: inulin, FOS and GOS, the only three the deck says you can call prebiotic with full confidence. All three are bifidogenic. Inulin's dose is 5 to 20 grams a day, FOS 5 to 21. GOS works at much lower doses, 1.4 to 7 grams, and the slide cites studies on IBS, traveller's diarrhoea and immunity. Competitor brands are named for each, such as Orafti, Frutalose and Bimuno.

Silver tier: resistant starch and PHGG. Resistant starch has over 200 human trials, but they vary, so specify the type and the endpoint; the dose range here is 3.5 to 30 grams a day. PHGG, at 5 to 7 grams, is low-FODMAP. The slide cites a trial of 108 people that reported less bloating than placebo, and notes a Health Canada IBS claim. The deck calls it a quiet workhorse for sensitive-gut positioning.

Bronze tier: low-dose and emerging fibres. Bronze means the human evidence is thin, not that the ingredient does not work. XOS raised bifidobacteria at 1.4 to 2.8 grams a day in one small study. Arabinoxylan from wheat has an EFSA glycaemia claim. For larch arabinogalactan the slide cites a trial of 199 people at 4.5 grams a day that reported fewer colds: 58.4% against 72.4%. Native guar is largely superseded by PHGG.

Benefit by benefit, cholesterol and blood glucose belong to the viscous fibres. For LDL cholesterol the claims sit at dose thresholds: beta-glucan at 3 grams a day or more, psyllium 7, pectin 6. For post-meal glucose: beta-glucan at 4 grams per 30 grams of carbohydrate, and pectin at 10 grams per meal. Inulin, FOS, acacia and wheat dextrin are not cholesterol ingredients; they lack the mechanism. For a cardiometabolic brief, reach for the viscous fibres.

Science is only half the choice; the other half is whether we can use it. Four formulation dials. Effective dose: how many grams does it take, since a low dose fits more formats. Taste: neutral, sweet or off-note. Ease of use: solubility, mouthfeel, grittiness and processing. Stability: does it survive heat, low pH and shelf life? A 10-gram fibre will not fit a capsule, a gummy or a small drink.

The winner sits where behaviour and formulation overlap. The worked example on this slide is a product the deck calls Advanced Biotics, which uses PHGG with GOS, the Bimuno brand. Both were chosen because they cleared validation, dose, taste and handling at once: low-dose, clinically validated, near-tasteless and easy to use. Higher-dose or off-tasting options failed the formulation dials. Do not pick the best on one dial; pick the one good enough on all.

Gas is the silent compliance-killer. Rapidly fermented short-chain prebiotics such as FOS and short-chain inulin ferment early in the colon and make gas, with a ceiling of about 5 to 10 grams in a single serving. The deck gives four solutions: blend short and long chains, use slow, well-tolerated fibres, choose ingredients that work at low doses, and build the dose up gradually. A product nobody can tolerate does not get bought again.

Here is the core difference in claims. "Dietary fibre" is a regulated label term: you can put it on the nutrition panel, and you can almost always say how many grams of fibre a product has. "Prebiotic" is not a regulated nutrient claim. In the US it is a structure-function descriptor; in the EU, UK and Canada it is treated as an implied health claim. Fibre is a number; prebiotic is a claim you must earn.

This is the deck's list of authorised claims to anchor on, each with its authority and dose. In the EU: beta-glucan for cholesterol, from 3 grams a day; glucomannan for weight loss within a calorie-restricted diet, 3 grams a day; pectin for cholesterol and glucose; and chicory inulin for normal defecation, from 12 grams a day. Psyllium's cholesterol claim and the RS2 type 2 diabetes claim are US FDA claims. Always quote the dose.

The market is big and growing, but treat the figures as directional. Prebiotics are put at 6 to 11 billion dollars and dietary fibre at 9 to 14 billion, from Grand View and FMI, and estimates vary two to threefold by definition. Inulin is the largest single prebiotic, at about 30 to 46% share, and gut health the largest segment, with Europe, at about 40%, and Asia-Pacific vying for the lead.

GLP-1 is the deck's highest-momentum white space. The slide gives about 30 million or more US adults who have taken a GLP-1 drug, about 18%, with 12% taking one now; digestive supplements up 52% among users, and weight-management formulas down 3% year on year. Fibre plays two roles: managing side effects such as constipation and tolerability, and what the deck calls a "fibre-first" GLP-1 secretion story, a mechanism it links to SCFAs.

This is the first half of the evidence master table: the Gold and Silver tiers, each with whether it is fibre, prebiotic or both, its key benefit and its dose. Gold includes psyllium, beta-glucan, inulin, FOS, GOS and resistant dextrin. Silver includes resistant starch, PHGG, resistant maltodextrin, polydextrose, acacia, pectin and glucomannan. Use it as a lookup when a brief names an ingredient.

The second half covers Bronze, the botanicals and the flagged ingredients. Here are XOS, arabinoxylan, HMOs and larch arabinogalactan, branded ingredients such as Solnul, AlphaGOS, Actazin and Livaux, and botanicals such as Eldercraft, 360GUT and Baobest. Note the flags: IMO is contested because it is largely digestible, and methylcellulose is fibre but not a prebiotic. Check the tier and dose before you recommend any of them.

This is the anchor list of authorised claims with their exact conditions. Beta-glucan: lowers cholesterol, at 3 grams a day. Oat beta-glucan: reduces the blood sugar rise after a meal, at 4 grams per 30 grams of carbohydrate. Pectin: maintenance of normal blood cholesterol, at 6 grams a day. Glucomannan: weight loss in a calorie-restricted diet, 3 grams a day. Chicory inulin: normal defecation, 12 grams a day. Psyllium and RS2 are FDA claims.

This table, and the next, are reproduced from the Global Prebiotic Association reference by Deehan and colleagues, 2024. They give examples of studies on established, novel and emerging prebiotics: the health effect, the dose and format used, and the outcome reported. This half covers acacia gum, FOS, GOS, HMOs and more. Read each row as one study's result, not as a claim we can make.

The second half of the reference table covers the novel and emerging tiers: omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols, resistant dextrin, resistant starch and xylans. Again, each row is a study: the effect looked at, the dose and format, and the outcome. The table comes from Deehan and colleagues, 2024, and that attribution stays with it whenever it is shown.

This is the quick pick: brief to shortlist. For a low-dose format, GOS, XOS or RS2. For a clear, stable drink, soluble corn fibre, resistant wheat dextrin, resistant maltodextrin or GOS. For a sensitive gut, PHGG, acacia or low-dose XOS. For a cardiometabolic claim, oat beta-glucan or psyllium. For a GLP-1 companion, PHGG, acacia or resistant dextrins. Keep it open in customer meetings.

Every commercial decision runs through one chain. Claim: what benefit do we want to say? Evidence: is it Gold, Silver or Bronze for that benefit? Dose: does the serving carry the studied dose? Format: can the format physically carry it? Jurisdiction: is the claim lawful in that market? If any link breaks, the claim breaks, and the break shows what to fix: the ingredient, the dose, the format, or the claim.

Our four priorities for the second half of 2026. Lead at the precision-prebiotic end: low-dose, validated, palatable ingredients such as PHGG, GOS, scFOS and XOS. Build the GLP-1 companion: gentle, nutrient-dense, tolerability-first products. Make credibility the moat: honest dosing, claims matched to evidence, and branded clinical ingredients. And secure precision-fermentation supply of HMOs, ahead of growth in adult nutrition.

lessons.summary:
This module introduces functional mushrooms: mushrooms valued for bioactive compounds rather than flavour, with a long
history in Traditional Chinese Medicine, Ayurveda and other traditions and now one of the fastest-growing sectors in
health and wellness. It covers the five the deck treats as key (reishi, lion's mane, cordyceps, chaga and turkey tail),
the benefits it associates with each, and the compounds behind them, from beta-glucans and triterpenoids to the
hericenones and erinacines of lion's mane and the cordycepin of cordyceps.

It explains the choice between fruiting body and mycelium, then where mushrooms are used: supplements, functional foods
and drinks such as mushroom coffee, nutricosmetics and sports nutrition. Retail data from SPINS shows mushrooms among
the fastest-growing functional ingredients in ready-to-drink and functional beverages.

The second half is about why our material is worth buying. Standardisation keeps bioactive levels consistent,
contamination testing covers heavy metals, mycotoxins and pesticides, and some mushrooms are grown on peanut substrates,
a hidden allergen risk. Our mushrooms are sourced on non-peanut substrates, which the deck calls a great USP. Quality,
transparency and allergen safety are its success factors.

sequence.script: Welcome to this training session on functional mushrooms and mushroom extracts. Over the next few slides, we’ll explore how these fascinating fungi have evolved from ancient remedies into modern nutraceutical and functional food powerhouses.

Our goals are to help you understand the unique biology of functional mushrooms, the health benefits they provide, and the ways they are extracted and processed.

We’ll also look at their applications in key industries like supplements, food and beverages, and beauty, while highlighting emerging trends and innovations that are shaping the market.

By the end of this session, you’ll have the tools and insights to confidently discuss the science, applications, and market potential of functional mushrooms with your customers or team.

Let’s start with the basics: what are functional mushrooms?

Unlike culinary mushrooms that are primarily used for flavor and nutrition, functional mushrooms are prized for their bioactive compounds, which deliver specific health benefits. These mushrooms have been used for centuries in traditional medicine systems like Traditional Chinese Medicine and Ayurveda.

Some key examples include reishi, known as the ‘mushroom of immortality’ for its calming and immune-boosting properties, and lion’s mane, famous for its potential to support brain health. Cordyceps is another popular functional mushroom, celebrated for its ability to enhance energy and endurance.

Functional mushrooms aren’t just a trend—they’ve transitioned from ancient remedies into modern wellness staples, appearing in everything from capsules and powders to coffees and skincare products.

Functional mushrooms have been a part of human culture for thousands of years, valued for their healing properties and therapeutic potential. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, reishi was referred to as the ‘mushroom of immortality,’ symbolizing longevity and vitality. Cordyceps, discovered by Tibetan herders, was traditionally used to improve energy and stamina, especially at high altitudes.

In Ayurvedic medicine, mushrooms like shiitake were used for their nourishing properties, while indigenous cultures worldwide incorporated mushrooms like chaga for immunity and resilience. These ancient practices have informed modern science, which continues to uncover and validate the health benefits of these incredible fungi.

Today, functional mushrooms are transitioning from traditional remedies to cutting-edge health and wellness products, thanks to advancements in extraction technologies and our understanding of their bioactive compounds.

Now that we’ve explored the history, let’s look at some of the most important functional mushrooms and their key benefits.

Reishi is known for its calming effects and immune-boosting properties, making it a popular choice in stress relief and immunity supplements.

Lion’s Mane supports cognitive health, with compounds like hericenones and erinacines shown to promote nerve growth factor, potentially aiding memory and focus.

Cordyceps enhances energy and endurance by improving oxygen uptake and ATP production, which makes it highly sought after in sports nutrition.

Chaga is packed with antioxidants that fight oxidative stress, making it a favorite for anti-aging and immune-boosting products.

Turkey Tail is valued for its polysaccharides, especially PSK and PSP, which are used in immune health and gut support.

Each of these mushrooms offers unique bioactive compounds that contribute to their health benefits and diverse applications.

It follows on from the five key mushrooms we've just met, and sets up the next slide, on which parts of the mushroom are used. Watch it as a buyer would: what should a good mushroom supplement be made from?

Next, a FreshCap Mushrooms video: what you need to know before you buy mushroom supplements. Watch for what separates one mushroom product from another, which leads into the next slide on fruiting body and mycelium.

To understand the benefits of functional mushrooms, we need to know which parts of the mushroom are used in extracts and why.

The fruiting body, which is the visible part of the mushroom, is often the most concentrated source of active compounds like beta-glucans, triterpenoids, and polysaccharides. This makes it ideal for immune, cognitive, and stress-related supplements.

The mycelium, which is the root-like structure beneath the surface, is also gaining popularity. While it has a different bioactive profile compared to fruiting bodies, it’s a scalable and cost-effective option for producing polysaccharides and ergothioneine, which are antioxidants.

Choosing between these parts depends on the desired health benefits, the cost of production, and the specific compounds being targeted. Both parts play important roles in creating high-quality mushroom extracts.

Functional mushrooms owe their health-promoting properties to a variety of bioactive compounds, each with unique benefits. These compounds are found in different mushrooms and often in specific parts, such as the fruiting body or mycelium.

Beta-glucans are perhaps the most widely recognized. They modulate the immune system by enhancing the activity of immune cells like macrophages and natural killer cells. Reishi, Turkey Tail, and Shiitake are particularly rich in beta-glucans.

Triterpenoids, abundant in Reishi and Chaga, have potent anti-inflammatory and adaptogenic effects. They help the body manage stress and support overall balance.

Polysaccharides, such as polysaccharopeptides (PSP) in Turkey Tail and lentinan in Shiitake, are known for their role in gut health and immune function.

Ergothioneine, a powerful antioxidant found in mycelium, protects cells from oxidative stress and supports anti-aging benefits.

Hericenones and Erinacines, unique to Lion’s Mane, are particularly notable for their ability to stimulate nerve growth factor (NGF), which is vital for cognitive health and memory.

Cordycepin, from Cordyceps, enhances energy production at the cellular level by improving oxygen uptake and ATP production. This makes it a favorite for sports nutrition products.

Melanin, found in Chaga, is an antioxidant that contributes to its potential skin-protective and anti-aging properties.

Below is processing: drying, freezing, canning, irradiation, pickling and packaging, which turn mushrooms into value-added products such as dehydrated mushroom, beverages, bakery products, soup powder, enriched flour and seasoning. On the right, the diagram labels areas of therapeutic potential, from antioxidant to gut health.

It comes after the summary of key mushrooms, their compounds and the benefits linked to them, and brings those together before we look at how mushrooms are used in products. Listen for the names you already know.
Next, FreshCap Mushrooms' beginner's guide to functional mushrooms. Watch for the mushrooms we've just covered; any benefits it mentions are the channel's own words, not claims we can make.

Functional mushrooms are incredibly versatile and have found applications across multiple industries.

In dietary supplements, they are widely used in capsules, powders, and tinctures targeting specific health concerns like immunity, cognition, and stress. Reishi, Lion’s Mane, and Cordyceps are key players here.

In the functional food and beverage sector, mushroom extracts are added to coffee, tea, and protein bars to deliver health benefits in convenient formats. For example, mushroom coffee blends with Cordyceps for energy and Reishi for relaxation are increasingly popular.

In nutricosmetics, mushrooms like Chaga and Reishi, rich in antioxidants, are used in beauty-from-within products, targeting skin health and anti-aging.

Finally, in sports nutrition, Cordyceps and Lion’s Mane are included in pre- and post-workout products for enhanced endurance, focus, and recovery.

These applications demonstrate the adaptability of functional mushrooms, making them a cornerstone ingredient in health and wellness innovations.

Here's what functional mushrooms look like on shelf. The slide shows mushroom coffees such as Four Sigmatic, Laird, Rheal and Motion; gummies from Dirtea; chocolate from Vital Leaf, Radek's and Cosmic Dealer; bars such as Lucid, Wise Bar, Aktivbar, Pro Shrooms and Balanced Tiger; and powders and capsules from brands like Spacegoods, Verve, Feel and OTO. Notice the range of formats: coffee, bars, chocolate and gummies sit right beside the capsules and powders.

All the data on this slide is from Spins. Mushrooms are among the fastest-growing functional ingredients in ready-to-drink and wider functional drinks. In RTD beverages, reishi grew 71% in dollars year on year, and cordyceps 52%. For lion's mane, kombucha and other functional beverages grew 158.2%; for turkey tail, the same category grew 226.6%. Overall, super mushroom sales in food and beverage reached 642 million dollars, up 19.5%, while vitamins and minerals fell 2.9% and body care fell 10.6%.

Quality and standardization are critical when it comes to functional mushroom products. Without proper standardization, the concentration of key bioactive compounds like beta-glucans or triterpenoids can vary significantly, impacting efficacy and consumer trust.

Standardized extracts ensure consistent levels of active compounds, making them more reliable for product formulation and health claims. For example, Reishi products are often standardized to contain a specific percentage of triterpenoids for stress and immune support.

Another key quality consideration is contamination. Mushrooms, particularly those grown in the wild, can accumulate heavy metals or toxins from their environment. Rigorous testing for contaminants, such as mycotoxins, pesticides, and heavy metals, is essential to meet regulatory standards and protect consumer safety.

Finally, sourcing and sustainability are becoming increasingly important to consumers. Using mushrooms grown in controlled environments ensures both purity and environmental responsibility, which are critical selling points in today’s market.

Allergen safety is a critical consideration in the production and sourcing of functional mushroom products. Some mushrooms, particularly those grown in mycelium form, are cultivated on substrates that may include peanuts or peanut shells. This can pose a significant risk to individuals with severe peanut allergies, a concern that should not be overlooked.

At Vita Actives, we prioritize allergen safety by sourcing mushrooms grown on non-peanut substrates, ensuring they are safe for a wider audience. This not only addresses consumer health concerns but also positions our products as more inclusive in the competitive marketplace.

By clearly communicating this allergen-friendly approach to customers, we can further build trust and differentiate our products, especially in markets where allergen labeling and transparency are top priorities.

The functional mushroom market is evolving rapidly, driven by consumer demand for innovative, effective, and sustainable products. One major trend is the growth of adaptogenic blends, which combine mushrooms like Reishi, Cordyceps, and Lion’s Mane with other botanicals to create synergistic effects for stress relief, energy, and focus.

Another trend is the expansion into new delivery formats, such as ready-to-drink beverages, effervescent tablets, and functional snacks like mushroom-infused bars and chips. These formats cater to on-the-go lifestyles and health-conscious consumers.

Sustainability and clean-label products are also driving innovation. Consumers increasingly prioritize mushrooms sourced from environmentally responsible farms, particularly organic and non-GMO options.

Finally, bioavailability-enhancing technologies, like liposomal delivery systems, are becoming more common, ensuring that the bioactives in mushrooms are absorbed efficiently by the body.

Functional mushrooms have transitioned from ancient remedies to modern wellness essentials, offering a wide range of health benefits and applications. By understanding their bioactive compounds, extraction methods, and market potential, we can better position ourselves in this growing industry.

Looking ahead, there are significant opportunities to explore. Personalized health solutions using mushroom-based formulations are gaining traction, allowing consumers to tailor products to their unique needs. The intersection of mushrooms and biohacking—a focus on longevity and optimized health—is another exciting frontier.

To succeed in this space, our focus should remain on quality, transparency, and innovation. By leveraging our non-peanut sourcing and commitment to sustainability, we can differentiate our products and meet the demands of today’s informed consumers.
